sources.news_title: Sudden Floods From Heavy Rains Cause Evacuations in Arizona and Colorado
sources.text:
Una nueva ronda de fuertes lluvias desató inundaciones repentinas y obligó a las autoridades a ordenar evacuaciones el domingo en una amplia franja del suroeste de estados Unidos, incluida una localidad montañosa de Colorado que tomaba medidas ante la posibilidad de que un río alcance niveles históricos. En tanto, los residentes de esta región normalmente árida se enfrentan con más ríos y arroyos desbordados.
En el suroeste de Colorado, las autoridades de la localidad de Pagosa Springs advirtieron en Facebook sobre posibles “inundaciones catastróficas”, debido a los pronósticos de que que el río San Juan alcance un máximo superior a los 5,8 metros (19 pies) a eso de las 11:00 de la noche del domingo.
“Para poner esa previsión en perspectiva: durante la devastadora inundación de 1911 que arrasó con la mayor parte de lo que existía como el pueblo de Pagosa en ese momento, el río San Juan alcanzó un máximo de aproximadamente 5,.4 metros (17,8 pies)”, señaló el Departamento de Policía del condado de Archuleta en Facebook. “Este es un evento de inundación potencialmente catastrófico. Se anticipan daños extensos”.
Las autoridades en la localidad turística de Sedona, Arizona, ordenaron la evacuación inmediata de residentes a las zonas cercanas a Oak Creek debido al rápido aumento en los niveles de inundaciones, las cuales dejaron a varias personas atrapadas al interior de sus viviendas. Funcionarios en el poblado cercano de Camp Verde también emitieron una orden de evacuación para residentes cerca del río Verde, el arroyo West Clear Creek y el arroyo Wet Beaver.
Arizona podría recibir el equivalente a 2 o 3 meses de lluvia en dos días “Recibiremos dos o tres meses de lluvia en el lapso de un par de días”, indicó Aaron Hardin, de la oficina del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional en Tucson, sobre las condiciones que han provocado inundaciones repentinas, posibles crecidas de ríos y rescates en botes rápidos en Tucson, a unos 370 kilómetros (230 millas) al sur de Sedona.
La más reciente ronda de intensas lluvias comenzó la noche del sábado y se anticipa que provoque inundaciones repentinas en zonas ya saturadas hasta el lunes. El servicio meteorológico estima que podrían caer hasta 10 centímetros (4 pulgadas) de lluvia en toda la región, impulsadas por una serie de sistemas de tormentas del Pacífico.
El servicio meteorológico emitió avisos por inundaciones para casi todo Arizona y partes del sur de Utah, el suroeste de Colorado y el oeste de Nuevo México, además de una buena del sur de Nevada. Eso incluye la región donde se encuentran Arizona, Colorado, Nuevo México y Utah.
Cierra carretera hacia localidad turística de Colorado Funcionarios de Pagosa Springs indicaron que cualquier persona que se encuentre en zonas bajas a lo largo de los ríos San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo y Piedra debe dirigirse a un albergue instalado en una iglesia local.
Indicaron que los residentes deben salir de inmediato, ya que el personal de emergencia podría estar sumamente limitado durante la parte más intensa de la tormenta. El camino que lleva a la localidad también se cerrará la tarde del domingo para el tráfico de entrada, indicaron las autoridades locales.
Katie German, propietaria y chef de Bruin Coffee en Pagosa Springs, comentó que el centro de la ciudad fue evacuado y que había calles inundadas. Añadió que lo que más le preocupa era que el único puente de acceso al pueblo sea arrasado.
“Todos estamos diciendo que Pagosa está cerrada porque van a cerrar la carretera a nuestros dos lados”, expresó German, quien cerró su tienda más temprano el domingo y cuyos padres tuvieron que evacuar hacia la vivienda de un hermano.
“Me preocupa mi negocio, me preocupan mis empleados, y definitivamente me preocupan todos en este pueblo”, afirmó. “Este pueblo, somos una comunidad muy, muy unida. Todos nos ayudamos”.
Equipos de emergencia en Arizona ayudan con rescates en Sedona En Sedona, las autoridades ordenaron a todos los residentes de zonas afectadas que se dirijan a la escuela secundaria Sedona Red Rock. Pero recomendaron a la población que no intente conducir por caminos con corrientes de agua y a mantenerse lejos de cauces y de los lechos secos por donde corre el agua.
El jefe del Distrito de Bomberos de Sedona, Ed Mezulis, publicó un breve video en Facebook en el que señaló que equipos de emergencia de comunidades cercanas estaban llegando para ayudar, debido a que los bomberos y la policía locales estaban copados respondiendo a varios reportes de residentes atrapados al interior de sus viviendas debido al aumento en los niveles del agua.
“Por favor, permanezcan en terreno alto, estén atentos a sus alertas y tengan cuidado”, aconsejó.
El departamento de bomberos difundió un video en el que se pueden ver potentes torrentes que inundan vehículos mientras corren con fuerza junto a viviendas y otras estructuras. Otros videos y fotos compartidos en redes sociales mostraban a personas de pie en un puente peatonal mientras toman fotos y videos de las turbulentas aguas marrones que corrían por debajo.
—-
Marcelo informó desde Nueva York y Casey desde Boston.

sources.news_title: El Nino Taking Aim At Southwest Today - Regional Media News
sources.text:
(Undated) – A stormy El Niño pattern is drenching the Southwest with rain today. A level three out of four flood risk has been issued for large portions of the region, including nearly all of central and northern Arizona. Parts of Colorado and New Mexico could also be hit hard. Moving into Monday, the storm will make its way into the Plains and Midwest, with a level one out of four flash flood threat spanning from Texas to Wisconsin.
Brought to you by www.srnnews.com

sources.news_title: Flash floods trigger evacuations in Arizona and Colorado amid heavy ra
sources.text:
More heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a wide swath of the Southwest on Sunday, including in a Colorado tourist town bracing for its main river to rise to historic levels, as weary residents in the normally arid region deal with another massive drenching.
In southwestern Colorado, officials in Pagosa Springs, a town of more than 2,000 in the Rockies located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs, warned in a Facebook post of potentially “catastrophic flooding” as the San Juan River was forecast to crest at more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) late Sunday night.
“To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters),” the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office said in a separate Facebook post . “This is a potentially catastrophic flood event.”
Officials in the tourist destination of Sedona, Arizona, ordered residents in areas near Oak Creek to leave immediately as flood waters rose rapidly and multiple people were trapped in their homes. Nearby Camp Verde also issued an evacuation order for residents living near the Verde River, West Clear Creek, and Wet Beaver Creek.
“We are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days,” said Aaron Hardin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Tucson.
The conditions produced flash floods, river flooding and swift boat rescues in Tucson, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of Sedona.
The latest round of soaking rains started Saturday evening and was expected to saturate the area through Monday. The weather service estimates as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.
The weather service issued flood warnings and watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet.
The weather service office for Salt Lake City said previous storms that soaked the area could contribute to excessive rain runoff during the latest downpours, especially in Washington County, Utah, and Zion and Capitol Reef National Parks.
“Flood prone areas will likely become inundated at times, and backcountry roads will likely become impassable from this excessive runoff,” a weather service statement said.
Officials in Pagosa Springs said anyone in low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra rivers should head to a designated shelter at a local church.
They advised residents not to wait to leave their homes as emergency crews may be extremely limited during the worst of the storm. The highway entering town also was closed to inbound traffic, and residents were advised to avoid contact with the San Juan River after sewage was discharged into it.
Katie German, owner and chef of Bruin Coffee in Pagosa Springs, said downtown had been evacuated and that there was street flooding. German said she was most worried about the one bridge into town washing out and trucks carrying everything from food to fuel not having a way in.
Town officials had just lifted an evacuation order from flooding last week only to reimpose it Saturday night with the San Juan forecast to crest Sunday night at 21.9 feet (6.7 meters), according to Vicki Shaffer, public information officer working the floods for the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office.
“I’m worried about my business, worried about my employees, definitely worried for everybody in this town,” German said. “This town, we’re a very, very, tight community. We all help each other out.”
Officials in La Plata County, which is west of Pagosa Springs, said all public roads were closed due to the flooding.
In Sedona, longtime resident Michelle Grimm worried about her community after viewing the rushing waters of Oak Creek rising perilously close to the underside of a pedestrian bridge near the center of town.
“I went out at eight this morning and I saw the bridge and I was like, ‘Oh, we’re in trouble,’” she said as she sheltered in place in her home Sunday afternoon.
“I’ve never seen them rescuing people with helicopters out of neighborhoods. I’ve never seen neighborhoods completely submerged in water,” Grimm said. “We’re just praying that the creek doesn’t rise anymore.”
Sedona officials on Sunday ordered residents living in affected areas to head to Sedona Red Rock High School, but they urged people not to attempt to drive across roads with rushing waters and to stay away from creek beds and washes.
Heavy rains forced the closure of several highways across Arizona, the state Department of Transportation reported .
Sedona Fire District Chief Ed Mezulis said in a short clip posted on Facebook that emergency crews from surrounding communities were coming in to assist as local fire and police officials were already responding to multiple reports of residents trapped in their homes.
“Please stay at high ground, watch your alerts and be careful,” he advised.
A video shared by the fire department showed powerful flood waters inundating vehicles and rushing past homes and other structures. Other videos and photos shared on social media showed people standing on a pedestrian bridge taking photos and videos as churning, brown waters rushed underneath .
—-
Marcelo reported from New York and Casey from Boston. Associated Press writer Christopher Weber in Los Angeles also contributed to this story.
